data.title: Bitcoin volatility gauges climb as traders pay up for protection
data.description:
Markets are falling, and the fear gauges are doing the opposite. Bitcoin's implied volatility indexes are climbing as investors pile into options to protect themselves against further declines.

It isn't only a crypto story. Stocks, gold, copper and currencies linked to commodity prices are all sliding together, and the indicators that track expected price swings are moving higher alongside them.

Implied volatility, or IV, is the market's estimate of how big future price moves will be. It is calculated from options prices, so it climbs when demand for options increases.

Deribit's DVOL, one of the most closely watched Bitcoin volatility gauges, stood at 46.0 on November 20, 2026. Through the period, it hovered at about 46%.

Block Scholes' BSIV index moved more sharply. It reached 51.6% after gaining 8.4 points, an increase of about 19% week-over-week.

Traditional markets are showing the same nerves. The VIX, Wall Street's best-known fear index, rose 22% to 25.43 as risk-off sentiment spread across asset classes.

The spike in implied volatility coincided with a slide in Bitcoin's spot price. Bitcoin dropped to around $61,450 in mid-to-late November 2026, which marked a multi-month low.

Money has also been leaving the Bitcoin exchange-traded funds. Outflows totaled $3.47 billion in November 2026 alone.

One single day accounted for $582 million of those withdrawals.

Options positioning points the same way. Put/call open-interest ratios show a strong preference for downside bets, meaning traders are holding more contracts that pay off if prices fall than contracts that pay off if they rise.

There's a useful comparison hiding in the data. Bitcoin's 30-day realized volatility, which measures how much the price has actually moved, was recorded at 33–44%.

That range still sits below where the implied gauges are trading. DVOL at 46 and BSIV at 51.6% are both above the top of the realized range.

When implied volatility runs ahead of realized volatility, traders are paying for movement that hasn't happened yet. They expect the next stretch to be rougher than the last one.

For anyone holding Bitcoin, the immediate takeaway is that hedging has gotten pricier. Buying puts now costs more than it did a week ago, because the volatility component of option premiums has risen.

The cross-asset nature of the selloff matters too. With the VIX at 25.43, this looks less like a crypto-specific problem and more like a broad retreat from risk.

The ETF flows are worth watching closely. A $3.47 billion monthly exodus, punctuated by a $582 million single-day outflow, shows that the investor base brought in through those funds can leave in size when sentiment sours.

Watch the spread between implied and realized volatility in the coming days. If realized volatility climbs to meet the 46 to 51.6% range priced into options, the hedgers will have been right to pay up. If price action stays within the 33–44% realized band, the volatility premium could deflate.

For now, the message from the options market is fairly blunt. With Bitcoin around $61,450 and fear gauges rising across asset classes, traders are positioning for turbulence and paying a premium to avoid being caught without cover.

data.title: GameStop has transformed from a meme stock into a 'real company,' analysts say
data.description:
By Bill Peters

Roaring Kitty's return had minimal impact on GameStop's stock, which has started to gain more sophisticated appeal for its 'new and improved story'

GameStop shares are up 34% so far this year.

After Roaring Kitty's reawakening on Thursday nudged GameStop's shares only modestly higher, some analysts are declaring the meme trade dead for the videogame and collectibles retailer.

The chain (GME), after being cast off by many analysts, no longer needs to rely simply on meme-stock energy for gains, according to Mike Hickey, an analyst at StoneX. Rather, shares stand to benefit from the ongoing collectibles boom and the launch of "Grand Theft Auto VI," as gamers download the game and upgrade their equipment to play it.

"It's a real company, and it's trading at what we think is a very undervalued price," Hickey said of GameStop.

When his firm previously covered GameStop, it had a sell rating and a price target of zero, he said. When the chain was swept up in the meme-stock frenzy, they stopped covering it, he noted: "But that trade is over."

Few analysts cover GameStop. But StoneX this month initiated coverage of GameStop shares with a buy rating and a $33 price target. Analysts there noted that the company, which over the years had closed hundreds of stores, stood to gain from select reopenings announced in September.

"September's announcement of selective U.S. store reopenings adds a new growth catalyst, while expanded collectibles space and dedicated fixtures could improve productivity within existing locations," the note said.

Dan Ives, senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co., echoed the optimism.

CEO Ryan Cohen "is turning GameStop into a collectibles story with massive efficiency," he said over email. "This is no longer a meme stock; it's in the process of becoming a new and improved story."

He added: "GameStop will still have many retail fans but we see it as a very undervalued asset."

On Thursday, a new post showing a picture of Cat Mario, appeared on the X account for Keith Gill, the investor known as Roaring Kitty, whose enthusiasm for GameStop created a retail-trading stampede into the stock in 2021. At the time, that ruined short sellers' bets against the company. But unlike previous spikes that followed arcane posts in years past, shares of GameStop only rose around 1.5% on Thursday.

Over the stock's roller-coaster journey since 2021, analysts have cast doubt on GameStop. They have cited losses, uneven sales, disruption from e-commerce and a shift toward online gaming. There are also general concerns about the videogame industry's ability to sustain demand as consumers struggle with higher prices for essentials. Some analysts have predicted that the chain might not survive the 2020s. And Wall Street questioned GameStop's efforts to buy or otherwise collaborate with eBay (EBAY).

In the second quarter, GameStop's sales fell 18.7% to $790.2 million. But revenue from collectibles - things like trading cards and action figures - jumped 57% and made up 45.1% of sales.

GameStop in September also raised its forecast for adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization - a profitability metric - to more than $650 million for its full fiscal year, which ends on Jan. 30.

The collectibles market has taken off thanks to nostalgia and the card industry's focus on rarities and limited drops. Quarterly sales of "Magic: The Gathering" have risen past $600 million, Hasbro (HAS), which makes the game, said last month. Shares of collectible figurine maker Funko (FNKO) have roughly doubled this year.

Shares of GameStop are up 34% over that period, and trading at around $27. That's still well off their 2021 highs. But Hickey still believes in the stock.

"There's really no other stock that you can buy that gives you that much exposure to collectibles, which we think is a durable opportunity," Hickey said.

"When we're out there talking to people, the first thing that people ask is, 'Are you serious? Isn't that a meme stock?'" he added. "We're serious as serious gets, and no, it's not a meme stock."

-Bill Peters

data.title: Belgian Consumer Confidence Remains Stable At -13
data.description:
BRUSSELS/FRANKFURT/PARIS (dpa-AFX) - Households in Belgium expressed an equally pessimistic attitude in November, the National Bank of Belgium said on Friday.

The consumer sentiment index stood at -13 in November, the same as in the previous month, which was the lowest reading since April 2025.

The sub-index measuring the expected economic situation in the country over the next twelve months improved slightly to -43 in November from -44 in October. The outlook regarding the financial situation of consumers over the next year also strengthened somewhat in November, with the corresponding index rising to -5 from -7.

Meanwhile, households' saving capacity remained unchanged, with the respective index standing at 18.

Consumers were significantly more pessimistic about unemployment, and the index rose to 23 from 19.

data.title: Anthropic soared in its debut as stocks tanked. Only one other IPO has done that since 1990.
data.description:
By Mark DeCambre

A look at what the S&P 500 did after that earlier IPO. Plus, a CoreWeave co-founder's bet on bonds, and why tech outages have people stocking up on food and cash.

👋🏽Happy Friday. Here's what I'm thinking about this morning: March 2008.

Bear Stearns had just unraveled. A few days later, Visa went public. Of all the weeks to do it.

Surprisingly, Visa shares rose nearly 30% on their first trading day. The S&P 500 fell 2.4%.

Anthropic pulled off something similar Thursday. Shares of the maker of the AI agent Claude ended the day well above their $83 offer price as the S&P, the Dow and the Nasdaq all fell by at least 2%.

I asked the Dow Jones Market Data team to look at IPOs that raised at least $5 billion. In records going back to 1990, Visa was the only other company whose shares gained on their first day during a market selloff that sharp.

So how did the S&P 500 fare after Visa's debut?

  • One week later: up 3.29%
  • One month later: up 7.08%
  • Three months later: up 3.42%
  • Six months later: down 3.34%
  • One year later: down 39.62%

Yesterday I wondered whether demand for Anthropic could lift the rest of Wall Street. Investors wanted a piece of the AI company and were more than willing to part with just about everything else.

Three stories worth your time ...

  • A co-founder of CoreWeave just made an unconventional $30 million wager on its battered bonds.

Following six losing days in a row for the S&P 500, Wall Street futures (ES00) (NQ00) are pointing to a seventh day of losses. Turns out restricting sales of the hottest product at the moment (semiconductors) to the second-largest economy (China) isn't good for business.

UnitedHealth shares are down nearly 20% over the past week. The Trump administration's pledge to crack down on Medicare Advantage fraud has taken a toll on the stock. Democratic proposals might generate greater headwinds.

After a week of tech outages, some households are putting aside extra groceries and other supplies - and cash. Here's what makes people want to stock up when the problems are online.

data.title: Nasdaq Futures Slide, Anthropic Shares Reverse IPO Gains — LITE, IREN, SNDK, NVDA In Focus
data.description:
Key points:
  • On Thursday, Wall Street’s three major indexes posted losses of more than 2%.
  • Lumentum and Iren remained under pressure as investors reassessed the outlook for AI infrastructure stocks and cloud spending.
  • SanDisk fell in premarket trading after TrendForce warned that NAND flash prices could weaken in 2027.

Stock futures traded mixed early on Friday, with losses from the previous session continuing to weigh on sentiment, as Anthropic’s (ANT) much-anticipated market debut failed to revive enthusiasm for artificial intelligence stocks.

S&P 500 futures fell 0.51%, while Nasdaq-100 futures dropped 1.37%. Dow Jones Industrial Average futures bucked the trend, gaining 0.12% as of 6:30 a.m. ET.

On Thursday, all three major U.S. benchmarks ended the session sharply lower. The Nasdaq Composite led the declines, shedding 2.25%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 2.19%, while the S&P 500 lost 2.02%.

ANT shares closed 17% higher after their market debut on Thursday, valuing the company at around $1.8 trillion. But the stock fell nearly 6% in early premarket trading, adding pressure to technology stocks.

Oil Prices Fall As Middle East Exports Ease Supply Fears

Oil prices fell on Friday and remained on track for a weekly decline, with strong exports from the Middle East outweighing concerns over supply disruptions following Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia’s capital, Riyadh, and reports of tanker disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz.

Brent crude futures dropped 0.75%, to $91.29 a barrel by 6.30 a.m. ET. US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude futures for December delivery fell 0.97%, to $82.40 a barrel.

The Tech Radar

Lumentum Holdings (LITE): Lumentum Holdings (LITE) came under further pressure after Marvell Technology’s (MRVL) declining share price eroded the value of its takeover offer, with Lumentum stock now down more than 40% since news of the deal emerged. CEO Michael Hurlston defended the agreement on Thursday, but analyst Gary Black said Tesla (TSLA) could face a similar selloff if SpaceX uses its stock to finance a potential acquisition. Based on Marvell’s Thursday closing price of $138.47, the offer was worth about $623 per Lumentum share, down from roughly $1,132 when the deal was announced. Black estimated Lumentum shares could be worth around $535, or 41% below their Oct. 28 closing price. The companies expect to complete the deal in the first half of 2028. LITE shares fell nearly 6% in early premarket trading Friday.

Iren (IREN): Shares extended their decline on Thursday, as concerns about the neocloud industry's growth prospects continued to weigh on the sector. The weakness persisted alongside a broader pullback in AI stocks, with Anthropic (ANT) also falling 5% in overnight trading after its strong market debut. Investors have grown increasingly cautious about Big Tech's cloud spending, the debt-heavy business models of neocloud providers and the sustainability of AI-related investment. Iren reported revenue of $228 million, up 66% sequentially, but delays in bringing some capacity online led Microsoft to spend less than it had planned in the previous quarter. IREN shares fell over 3% in premarket trading.

SanDisk Corp. (SNDK): Shares slipped over 6% in premarket trading as TrendForce warned that NAND flash prices could come under pressure in 2027, with order cuts by Chinese cloud providers potentially outweighing demand growth in the U.S. The firm expects NAND contract prices to decline 0% to 5% quarter over quarter in the first quarter of 2027, with prices falling across all product categories from the second quarter. Industry capital spending is projected to rise 26.7% to $29.9 billion, while the shift to QLC and higher-layer NAND technology could boost bit supply by 25% to 30%. Enterprise SSDs remain a key growth driver, but weakening demand from major Chinese cloud providers could weigh on the market. The outlook comes as SanDisk completes its 8-for-1 stock split.

Trending Stocks

Anthropic (ANT): Shares of the Claude maker fell 7.4% in premarket trading Friday, giving back some of their gains after surging 17% in their Nasdaq debut a day earlier. Anthropic raised $81.3 billion in what became the largest initial public offering on record, surpassing SpaceX’s June debut. The stock opened at $111.50 before closing Thursday at $97.17.

Nvidia (NVDA): Shares slipped 2.4% in premarket trading Friday amid concerns over CEO Jensen Huang’s departure and leadership succession, and California's scrutiny of potential chip diversions to China. Separately, New York University finance professor Aswath Damodaran called Huang a “great CEO” and said he would consider buying Nvidia shares below $140. He also weighed in on potential successors to the longtime chief executive.

What Else To Watch On Friday

On Friday, investors will look to the final reading of the University of Michigan’s consumer sentiment index for the month.

SPY, QQQ, DIA: Retail Sentiment

Retail sentiment toward the SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY), which tracks the S&P 500, slipped to ‘neutral’ from ‘bullish’ over the past 24 hours. Sentiment toward the SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF Trust (DIA) remained ‘bearish,’ while the Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ), which tracks the Nasdaq-100, continued to carry a ‘bullish’ rating. Both DIA and QQQ sentiment were unchanged over the same period.

data.title: MasTec to Buy Mechanical Contractor Murphy for $1.25 Billion
data.description:
By Colin Kellaher

MasTec has agreed to buy mechanical contractor Murphy Corp. for $1.25 billion in cash a deal that bolsters the infrastructure engineering and construction company's position in the growing mission-critical infrastructure markets.

MasTec on Friday said Murphy provides mechanical, plumbing and process infrastructure solutions across end markets that include aviation and defense, pharmaceutical, healthcare, technology and advanced manufacturing.

Murphy expects to generate revenue of about $775 million and adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization this year, MasTec said, adding that it expects to complete the acquisition expeditiously.

MasTec last month forecast 2026 revenue of $18.3 billion and adjusted Ebitda of $1.565 billion to $1.6 billion.

The Coral Gables, Fla., company said it plans to fund the acquisition, which includes a potential earnout payment based on Murphy's cumulative three-year financial performance, with a bank term loan.

data.title: MasTec to acquire mechanical contractor Murphy for about $1.25B
data.description:
MasTec on Friday said it will acquire mechanical contractor Murphy for roughly $1.25 billion in cash.

The company said the deal will boost MasTec’s business in mission-critical infrastructure markets, including aviation and defense, pharmaceutical, healthcare, technology, and advanced manufacturing.

“Murphy expands MasTec’s capabilities in some of the fastest-growing and most diverse infrastructure markets in North America. Its highly skilled union craft workforce, supported by established apprenticeship, training and field-leadership programs, provides the labor capacity and execution expertise required to deliver large, complex projects safely and efficiently,” said MasTec’s Chief Executive Officer Jose Mas.

Murphy will serve as a new operating group of MasTec, and Murphy’s financial results are expected to be reflected in the Clean Energy and Infrastructure Segment, MasTec said. Murphy's management team, led by President and Chief Executive Officer Patrick Murphy, will remain in place following the transaction.

MasTec said there is a potential earnout payment based on the cumulative three-year financial performance of Murphy post-closing.

Murphy is projected to generate full calendar year 2026 revenue and an adjusted EBITDA of about $775 million and roughly $140 million, respectively, it added.

Shares of MasTec, which is an infrastructure engineering and construction company, were down over 1% in premarket trading.

data.title: EM equities eye biggest weekly drop since 2020 on AI rout, rate concerns
data.description:
Key points:
  • EM equities suffer worst week since 2020
  • EM debt suffers biggest outflow since 2020
  • Hungary's wage deal offers support to consumption

By Tharuniyaa Lakshmi

Emerging market stocks were on track for their biggest weekly drop since the COVID-19 pandemic selloff of 2020, as worries over a potential AI slowdown hammered tech-heavy Asian markets on Friday, while the prospects of higher US interest rates kept currencies under pressure.

Stocks in Taiwan TWSE:TAIEX plunged 6% to record their biggest weekly decline since 1990, while South Korea's Kospi fell more than 5% as investors unwound AI-linked bets across the globe despite a record-breaking debut for Anthropic and strong forecasts from chip giant Nvidia .

Tech stocks across the globe have sold off sharply in recent weeks as worries about tighter US regulation on data centre development and chip exports as well as the abrupt exit of Jensen Huang as Nvidia's CEO fuelled concerns about the future of AI, especially after explosive growth in the technology boosted stock markets and economies this year.

MSCI's emerging market equities index CBOE:EFS fell 3%, on track to wipe out most of its year-to-date gains, in a sharp reversal from mid-June when it was up nearly 29%.

"The pillars of EM leadership are shifting. AI powered an exceptional 2026, but higher funding costs increasingly expose the ROIC-destructive economics of hyperscaler capex," Jefferies analysts said.

"A moderation in AI investment could trigger EM earnings downgrades, led by Korea and Taiwan, while India and China offer relative earnings resilience."

Indian stocks , have been a rare bright spot, trading at nine-month highs, helped by a relative lack of exposure to AI companies and a sharp retreat in oil prices.

Equity markets in emerging Europe dropped too, with Poland's WIG20 down nearly 3% and Hungary's Budapest SE index falling 2.3%.

US RATE WORRIES

The MSCI EM currencies index (.MIEM00000CUS) dipped 0.1% and was set for its fourth consecutive weekly decline.

In South Africa, the rand hovered just below one-year lows against the dollar, on increasing bets on US interest rate hikes and the South African central bank's decision to keep interest rates unchanged. The currency steadied at 17.45 per dollar, having touched a one-year low of 17.56 earlier in the session.

Investor caution was also evident in debt markets, with Bank of America data showing EM debt funds recorded outflows of $7.5 billion in the latest week ending November 18, the largest withdrawal since April 2020.

In Hungary, meanwhile, the government said gross minimum wages would rise by 7.5% to 347,000 forints ($1,020.44) next year under an agreement reached late on Thursday with employers and trade unions, offering some support to domestic demand prospects.

The Hungarian forint weakened 0.3% against the euro, as investors awaited Moody's review of Hungary's sovereign rating later in the day.

The Polish zloty fell 0.4% amid fading hopes for a breakthrough in Ukraine. Polish authorities said they were investigating reports that at least two unidentified objects had fallen near the Ukrainian border after the military said the country's airspace may have been violated during Russian strikes on Ukraine.​‌

Investors were also keeping a close watch on developments in the Middle East.

Brent crude fell nearly 1% as robust crude exports from the Middle East eased supply concerns, overshadowing Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia's capital Riyadh and reports of tanker disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz.​‌

data.title: GE Aerospace Warns Shareholders Against Potemkin's Mini-Tender Offer
data.description:
WASHINGTON (dpa-AFX) - GE Aerospace (GE), an aerospace and defense company, Friday said it has received notice of an unsolicited mini-tender offer by Potemkin Limited to purchase up to 10,000 of its shares for $186 per share in cash. The offer represents less than 0.001% of the company's outstanding shares.

Mini-tender offers seek to acquire less than 5% of a company's outstanding shares and are therefore subject to fewer disclosure and procedural requirements under U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission rules than larger tender offers.

Potemkin's offer price is 34.88% below its closing share price of $285.64 on October 23, 2026, the last trading day before the offer commenced. It is also 41.67% below the stock's closing price of $318.88 on November 19, 2026.

The company said it does not endorse the offer and has advised shareholders not to tender their shares, citing the significant discount to the current market price.

GE Aerospace recommended that shareholders who have already tendered their shares withdraw them in accordance with Potemkin's offering documents.

The SEC has cautioned investors that mini-tender offers may catch shareholders off guard and result in securities being sold at below-market prices.

In pre-market trading on the NYSE, GE Aerospace shares are down 0.55% after closing at $318.88 on Thursday.

data.title: AI Stocks Tumble Across the Globe as Slowdown Fears Mount
data.description:
By Joe Stonor

Artificial intelligence stocks fell across the globe as sentiment around the AI trade deteriorated further, despite Anthropic's record-breaking IPO Thursday.

Nasdaq futures were 1.3% lower as the index headed toward its worst one-week performance since President Trump's April 2025 imposition of sweeping tariffs. Chip makers and cloud-computing stocks sold off. Intel and Micron Technology fell 4.5% and 5.2% premarket, respectively, while Advanced Micro Devices tumbled 6.2%, extending a sharp fall from the last session following a short-seller report into the company published Thursday. Stocks that benefit from the build-out in AI suffered too, with data center power-supplier Caterpillar down 2.5% premarket.

Tech giants that served as havens in previous AI wobbles provided no safety premarket, with Meta Platforms and Microsoft both falling more than 1%.

So-called Animal spirits are taking over the market, XTB's Kathleen Brooks said. Multiple fears are weighing on investors' outlook, the research director said, including worries about high financing costs, excessive AI spending and legislation that could hurt the technology in the U.S.

Combined, those factors threaten a pullback in the AI build-out that could lead to lower revenues for related companies.

Asian stocks were hit hard Friday. South Korean memory-chip makers Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix fell 7% and 5.9%, respectively. In Japan, SoftBank Group--a major backer of OpenAI--fell 14.5%.

Europe's most valuable company, Dutch supplier of chip-making equipment ASML, fell close to 6%, putting it on track to lose around 28 billion euros of market value ($30.71 billion). A gauge of the continent's tech sector fell 3.6%.

Anthropic itself was down more than 6.5% premarket to trade around $90.80 a share. Adding to pressure on the stock was news, first reported by Bloomberg, that Apple is developing a new autonomous AI agent. The consumer-focused product could offer fresh competition to Anthropic's models.

Analysts are also concerned that Anthropic's revenue growth won't be enough to significantly outpace its spending commitments. The model maker has spending commitments totaling $900.9 billion, around half of which are due over the next five years, according to its IPO filing with the SEC.

"We are concerned about Anthropic's revenue growth," Seaport Research senior analyst Jay Goldberg wrote in a note. "To merit its valuation, it will need to see much higher growth rates over the next two years."

Investors are ditching AI stocks over fears that the sector's spending boom has passed its peak "in spite of a lack of any compelling evidence as yet of any such development on the ground," Jefferies' global head of equity strategy, Christopher Wood, said.

Driving the fear are concerns that Nvidia will step back from its role as financier-in-chief for the wider AI ecosystem, Wood said. In particular, investors worry Nvidia will pull its backing of chip-hungry cloud-computing startups, Wood said.

"This suggests a real risk that the most speculative part of the demand for compute will disappear which should lower compute prices for others."
